Reference: Hsiao (2026)

Model Setting

The paper asks how well trade policy can substitute for domestic environmental regulation when the emitting country will not or cannot regulate. The application is palm oil: land clearing for plantations destroys carbon-rich tree biomass and peat deposits in Indonesia and Malaysia, which together account for 84 percent of world production and 89 percent of exports, and palm oil accounts for about 5 percent of global CO2 emissions from 1990 to 2016. Two obstacles limit trade policy. The first is a coordination problem: tariffs imposed by a subset of importers lower world prices and raise consumption in unregulated markets (leakage). The second is a commitment problem: once forest is cleared, emissions are sunk, so regulation is no longer statically optimal, and forward-looking producers respond weakly to tariffs that they expect to lapse. The framework combines a static almost ideal demand system for vegetable oils in four consumer markets (the EU, China and India, other importers, and Indonesia and Malaysia) with a dynamic discrete-continuous model of mill entry and plantation development at 2,050 sites, using annual data for 1988 to 2016. Demand elasticities determine the losses from non-coordination, and the gap between short- and long-run supply elasticities determines the losses from non-commitment. Sites are k-means clusters of satellite-mapped plantations around observed mills (target density of one mill per 535 square kilometers). By 2016, 72 percent of sites have a mill, plantation area has grown from 2.4 to 19.9 million hectares, and the average site stores 1,626 tons of CO2 per hectare (386 in tree biomass and 1,240 in peat), so carbon damages outweigh revenues for any social cost of carbon above 12 dollars per ton.

Supply: Choices and States

Each site iii is a small, independent, forward-looking firm with rational expectations, and there is no exit or scrappage. A site makes a binary extensive-margin choice mit∈{0,1}m_{it}\in\{0,1\}mit​∈{0,1} to construct a mill and a continuous intensive-margin choice nitn_{it}nit​ of how much land to deforest and develop into plantations. The mill stock MitM_{it}Mit​ and mature plantation acreage NitN_{it}Nit​ follow:

Mit+1=Mit+mit,Nit+3=Nit+2+nit(4)M_{it+1}=M_{it}+m_{it},\qquad N_{it+3}=N_{it+2}+n_{it} \tag{4}Mit+1​=Mit​+mit​,Nit+3​=Nit+2​+nit​(4)

so newly planted land bears fruit only after three years (time to build). Policy, Emissions and Welfare

Regulation takes the form of ad valorem taxes on palm oil. Domestic regulation imposes production taxes τgtS>0\tau^S_{gt}>0τgtS​>0 that can vary by producing region. Import tariffs and export taxes impose consumption taxes τktD>0\tau^D_{kt}>0τktD​>0 that can vary by consumer market. The palm oil market clearing condition becomes:

∑kq1ktD((1+τktD)p1t,p2t)=∑iq1itS((1−τg1S)p11,…,(1−τgTS)p1T)∀t(13)\sum_kq^D_{1kt}\left(\left(1+\tau^D_{kt}\right)p_{1t},p_{2t}\right)=\sum_iq^S_{1it}\left(\left(1-\tau^S_{g1}\right)p_{11},\ldots,\left(1-\tau^S_{gT}\right)p_{1T}\right)\qquad\forall t \tag{13}k∑​q1ktD​((1+τktD​)p1t​,p2t​)=i∑​q1itS​((1−τg1S​)p11​,…,(1−τgTS​)p1T​)∀t(13)

Consumers in market kkk pay (1+τktD)p1t(1+\tau^D_{kt})p_{1t}(1+τktD​)p1t​ and producers in region ggg receive (1−τgtS)p1t(1-\tau^S_{gt})p_{1t}(1−τgtS​)p1t​, so a tariff of 100 percent matches a production tax of 50 percent: in both cases consumers pay twice what producers receive. Coordination means applying taxes across all regions or markets. Incomplete coverage of regions creates supply-side leakage, as production shifts toward untaxed regions when world prices rise. Incomplete coverage of markets creates demand-side leakage, as tariffs lower p1tp_{1t}p1t​ and unregulated consumption rises. Import tariffs also never reach consumers in Indonesia and Malaysia. Commitment means applying taxes over time. Taxes today are costly but prevent no emissions: existing development is sunk, and new development does not produce taxable output until time to build has elapsed. Only taxes expected tomorrow deter clearing today, but tomorrow that clearing is sunk as well, so the static incentive is always to set taxes to zero. In the counterfactuals, tax rates are announced at the outset, are constant during an initial commitment period, and lapse to zero afterwards; the dynamic game between policymakers and producers is not modeled, and palm oil is taxed uniformly. Plantation development is assumed to release carbon stocks fully. Writing eie_iei​ for the carbon stock density of site iii (tree biomass plus peat), cumulative palm emissions over the study period are:

E=∑t∑ieinit(14)E=\sum_{t}\sum_ie_in_{it} \tag{14}E=t∑​i∑​ei​nit​(14)

Welfare changes relative to business as usual and the abatement cost reported in the paper are:

ΔWk=ΔCSk+ΔPSk+ΔGRk,abatement cost=∑kΔWkΔE(15)\Delta W_k=\Delta CS_k+\Delta PS_k+\Delta GR_k,\qquad\text{abatement cost}=\frac{\sum_k\Delta W_k}{\Delta E} \tag{15}ΔWk​=ΔCSk​+ΔPSk​+ΔGRk​,abatement cost=ΔE∑k​ΔWk​​(15)

where consumer surplus CSkCS_kCSk​ is the compensating variation needed to maintain baseline utility, producer surplus PSkPS_kPSk​ is revenue net of costs (zero for importers), and government revenue GRkGR_kGRk​ is the product of tax rates, prices and quantities. A global social planner with social cost of carbon SCCSCCSCC favors a policy when SCC⋅(−ΔE)+∑kΔWk>0SCC\cdot(-\Delta E)+\sum_k\Delta W_k>0SCC⋅(−ΔE)+∑k​ΔWk​>0.

Estimation: Demand

Demand parameters enter nonlinearly through PktP_{kt}Pkt​, so the paper uses the iterated linear least squares estimator of Blundell and Robin (1999). For fixed price index values Pkt0P^0_{kt}Pkt0​, the share equation is linear:

ωokt=∑o^αoo^kln⁡po^t+γok0+γok1t+δokln⁡(XktPkt0)+εokt(16)\omega_{okt}=\sum_{\hat{o}}\alpha_{o\hat{o}k}\ln p_{\hat{o}t}+\gamma^0_{ok}+\gamma^1_{ok}t+\delta_{ok}\ln\left(\frac{X_{kt}}{P^0_{kt}}\right)+\varepsilon_{okt} \tag{16}ωokt​=o^∑​αoo^k​lnpo^t​+γok0​+γok1​t+δok​ln(Pkt0​Xkt​​)+εokt​(16)

The procedure starts from ln⁡Pkt0=ln⁡Xkt−ln⁡Qkt\ln P^0_{kt}=\ln X_{kt}-\ln Q_{kt}lnPkt0​=lnXkt​−lnQkt​ with Qkt=∑oqoktQ_{kt}=\sum_oq_{okt}Qkt​=∑o​qokt​, estimates the linear equation on palm oil shares (imposing adding-up, homogeneity and symmetry), recomputes the translog index from the estimates, and repeats until convergence, separately for each market. Prices are endogenous because εokt\varepsilon_{okt}εokt​ raises demand and therefore prices. The instruments are weather shocks to vegetable oil production, which act as supply shifters: for each crop and producing province, total absolute deviations of daily rainfall and temperature from crop-specific optimal conditions during the growing season, aggregated with production weights. Palm weather shocks instrument for palm prices and other-oil weather shocks for other-oil prices. The exclusion restriction is that these narrowly defined shocks affect demand only through prices and not through income or expenditure. Standard errors are Newey-West. Elasticities are computed by raising palm oil prices by 1 percent in every year and reporting the percentage change in total consumption over the study period.

Estimation: Supply

Supply is estimated with Euler methods (Hall 1978; Scott 2013), so the model is estimated without solving it. On the intensive margin, the value function is differentiated with respect to nitn_{it}nit​ and nit+1n_{it+1}nit+1​, and continuation values difference out by the envelope theorem. A hectare developed in ttt rather than t+1t+1t+1 earns one additional year of revenue, in t+3t+3t+3, so marginal development costs in adjacent years satisfy (in expectation given sits_{it}sit​):

γg0+γg1t+xiδ+εit+ψnit=αβ3pt+3yit+3+β(γg0+γg1(t+1)+xiδ+εit+1+ψnit+1)(17)\begin{aligned} &\gamma^0_g+\gamma^1_gt+x_i\delta+\varepsilon_{it}+\psi n_{it}\\ &\qquad=\alpha\beta^3p_{t+3}y_{it+3}+\beta\left(\gamma^0_g+\gamma^1_g(t+1)+x_i\delta+\varepsilon_{it+1}+\psi n_{it+1}\right) \end{aligned} \tag{17}​γg0​+γg1​t+xi​δ+εit​+ψnit​=αβ3pt+3​yit+3​+β(γg0​+γg1​(t+1)+xi​δ+εit+1​+ψnit+1​)​(17)

Rearranging and replacing expectations with realizations gives the first regression equation:

nit−βnit+1=αβ3ψpt+3yit+3+βψγg1−1−βψ(γg0+γg1t+xiδ)+μit+ηit(18)n_{it}-\beta n_{it+1}=\frac{\alpha\beta^3}{\psi}p_{t+3}y_{it+3}+\frac{\beta}{\psi}\gamma^1_g-\frac{1-\beta}{\psi}\left(\gamma^0_g+\gamma^1_gt+x_i\delta\right)+\mu_{it}+\eta_{it} \tag{18}nit​−βnit+1​=ψαβ3​pt+3​yit+3​+ψβ​γg1​−ψ1−β​(γg0​+γg1​t+xi​δ)+μit​+ηit​(18)

Earlier development brings added revenue and avoids rising cost trends, while later development delays and discounts costs. On the extensive margin, the mill value function is differenced with respect to mitm_{it}mit​ and mit+1m_{it+1}mit+1​. Continuation values cancel by finite dependence (Arcidiacono and Miller 2011): mill construction and plantation development are terminal actions, so whether a site invests in ttt or t+1t+1t+1, mills are operational and plantations have matured by t+4t+4t+4. With conditional choice probabilities πit\pi_{it}πit​ of mill construction:

ln⁡(πit1−πit)−βln⁡πit+1=12ψnit2+βγˉg1−(1−β)(γˉg0+γˉg1t+xiδˉ)+μˉit+ηˉit(19)\ln\left(\frac{\pi_{it}}{1-\pi_{it}}\right)-\beta\ln\pi_{it+1}=\frac{1}{2}\psi n_{it}^2+\beta\bar{\gamma}^1_g-(1-\beta)\left(\bar{\gamma}^0_g+\bar{\gamma}^1_gt+x_i\bar{\delta}\right)+\bar{\mu}_{it}+\bar{\eta}_{it} \tag{19}ln(1−πit​πit​​)−βlnπit+1​=21​ψnit2​+βγˉ​g1​−(1−β)(γˉ​g0​+γˉ​g1​t+xi​δˉ)+μˉ​it​+ηˉ​it​(19)

where 12ψnit2\frac{1}{2}\psi n_{it}^221​ψnit2​ embodies the added plantation profits from earlier entry. The residuals contain expectational errors ηit,ηˉit\eta_{it},\bar{\eta}_{it}ηit​,ηˉ​it​ and structural errors:

μit=−1ψεit+βψεit+1,μˉit=−εˉit+βεˉit+1(20)\mu_{it}=-\frac{1}{\psi}\varepsilon_{it}+\frac{\beta}{\psi}\varepsilon_{it+1},\qquad\bar{\mu}_{it}=-\bar{\varepsilon}_{it}+\beta\bar{\varepsilon}_{it+1} \tag{20}μit​=−ψ1​εit​+ψβ​εit+1​,μˉ​it​=−εˉit​+βεˉit+1​(20)

The two equations are stacked and estimated jointly. The intensive equation identifies {α/ψ,γg0/ψ,γg1/ψ,δ/ψ}\{\alpha/\psi,\gamma^0_g/\psi,\gamma^1_g/\psi,\delta/\psi\}{α/ψ,γg0​/ψ,γg1​/ψ,δ/ψ} given the discount factor, which is not identified (Magnac and Thesmar 2002) and is set to β=0.9\beta=0.9β=0.9. The extensive equation identifies {ψ,γˉg0,γˉg1,δˉ}\{\psi,\bar{\gamma}^0_g,\bar{\gamma}^1_g,\bar{\delta}\}{ψ,γˉ​g0​,γˉ​g1​,δˉ}, which isolates ψ\psiψ and delivers the remaining parameters in levels. The revenue coefficient α\alphaα is identified by combining time-series variation in world prices with spatial variation in yields: if supply is elastic, high-yield sites develop more aggressively than low-yield sites when prices rise, with zero-yield sites as the natural normalization.

Three problems arise in the intensive equation. Future revenue pt+3yit+3p_{t+3}y_{it+3}pt+3​yit+3​ may be correlated with μit\mu_{it}μit​ if unobserved costs contain aggregate shocks that move future prices; it is mechanically correlated with ηit\eta_{it}ηit​, which includes E[pt+3yit+3∣sit]−pt+3yit+3\mathbb{E}[p_{t+3}y_{it+3}\mid s_{it}]-p_{t+3}y_{it+3}E[pt+3​yit+3​∣sit​]−pt+3​yit+3​; and μit\mu_{it}μit​ is autocorrelated. The paper instruments pt+3yit+3p_{t+3}y_{it+3}pt+3​yit+3​ with ZtyitZ_ty_{it}Zt​yit​, where the demand shifters ZtZ_tZt​ are total vegetable oil consumption outside Indonesia and Malaysia (the category budget) and weather shocks to other vegetable oil production (residual demand for palm oil). Because these instruments are dated ttt, rational expectations make them orthogonal to ηit\eta_{it}ηit​. Standard errors are clustered by district. The intensive equation uses sites with Mit+mit=1M_{it}+m_{it}=1Mit​+mit​=1 and the extensive equation uses sites with Mit=0M_{it}=0Mit​=0, for which πit\pi_{it}πit​ is computed nonparametrically with cubic splines in latitude, longitude, cost factors and time, and nitn_{it}nit​ is imputed by smoothing over observed choices under the assumption that unobserved mill and plantation costs are uncorrelated. The approach requires atomistic, independent sites and no age effects on profits, but no specification of long-run expectations.

Key Estimates

  • Demand: IV own-price elasticities of palm oil are −0.723-0.723−0.723 (EU), −0.692-0.692−0.692 (China and India), −0.876-0.876−0.876 (other importers) and −0.925-0.925−0.925 (Indonesia and Malaysia), so demand is inelastic but leakage remains. OLS estimates are biased toward zero (−0.209-0.209−0.209 for the EU). The own-price share coefficients α11k\alpha_{11k}α11k​ are small (0.041 for the EU).

  • Supply: the price coefficient is α=2.994×10−8\alpha=2.994\times10^{-8}α=2.994×10−8. Median costs are 8,039 dollars per hectare of plantation and 91.15 million dollars per mill, plus about 1,522 dollars per hectare from convexity (ψ/α\psi/\alphaψ/α of 6.56 dollars, times one half, times the average nitn_{it}nit​ of 464 hectares). Plantation costs fall by 5 percent of median costs per year and mill costs rise by 1.5 percent.

  • Cost factors: one more kilometer from a major road, port or urban area raises mill costs by 0.38 percent of median costs but has no effect on the intensive margin. Carbon stocks have negligible effects, so producers internalize transport costs but not emission externalities.

  • Elasticities: the supply elasticity of total production over the study period is 1.3 for a price change sustained from 1988 to 2001 and 2.8 for one sustained from 1988 to 2016. OLS estimates are biased downward, and a static version yields small and negative elasticities.

Solving the Model

Counterfactuals require the model in levels. The paper sets εˉit=εit=εokt=0\bar{\varepsilon}_{it}=\varepsilon_{it}=\varepsilon_{okt}=0εˉit​=εit​=εokt​=0 and zero expectational errors, and computes continuation values up to the terminal year 2050, assuming linear growth in yields and in the supply of other oils, annual inflation of 2 percent, and expenditure growth Xkt+1=(1+λ)XktX_{kt+1}=(1+\lambda)X_{kt}Xkt+1​=(1+λ)Xkt​. The growth rate λ\lambdaλ, interpreted as expected long-run growth in aggregate demand, is chosen so that equilibrium prices best fit observed palm oil prices, giving λ^=0.106\hat{\lambda}=0.106λ^=0.106. Because Indonesia and Malaysia supply 84 percent of output, their production is scaled by factors Ωt\Omega_tΩt​ such that D1t=S1tΩtD_{1t}=S_{1t}\Omega_tD1t​=S1t​Ωt​, with Ω2016=1.1\Omega_{2016}=1.1Ω2016​=1.1 applied beyond the study period. The model matches prices and quantities in levels and trends and tracks cumulative emissions, although it misses the large emission episodes of the late 2000s.

Counterfactuals

All effects are totals for 1988 to 2016 relative to business as usual, with welfare in year-2000 dollars. Long-run policies are upheld from 1988 to 2016 and short-run policies from 1988 to 2001.

  • Domestic regulation: a coordinated, long-run production tax of 50 percent cuts emissions by 7.4 Gt (0.26 Gt per year) at a global cost of 13 dollars per ton. Importers lose (21 billion for the EU, 40 for China and India, 73 for other importers), but Indonesia and Malaysia gain 38 billion through terms-of-trade manipulation; their welfare is maximized at 9.3 Gt of abatement (a 60 percent tax). Unilateral taxes cut 4.8 Gt (Indonesia) and 1.7 Gt (Malaysia), the latter undone by elastic Indonesian supply. The coordinated short-run tax cuts only 0.8 Gt, at 38 dollars per ton.

  • Import tariffs: coordinated, long-run tariffs of 100 percent cut emissions by 5.4 Gt (0.19 Gt per year), less than the production tax because domestic consumers are untaxed. All importers gain (8.6, 9.4 and 13 billion) while Indonesia and Malaysia lose 88 billion. With compensating transfers that leave every non-EU market weakly better off, the cost to the EU is 15 dollars per ton; tariffs of 350 percent reach 9.4 Gt at less than 25 dollars per ton.

  • Coordination: long-run tariffs by an EU-China-India coalition cut 2.1 Gt and by the EU alone 0.7 Gt. At a target cost of 25 dollars per ton, the coalition reaches only 2.4 Gt (tariffs of 125 percent) and the EU alone 0.5 Gt (tariffs of 50 percent). Unilateral action can still deliver 1 Gt at 50 dollars per ton.

  • Commitment: coordinated short-run tariffs cut at most 0.5 Gt, since producers look toward high post-tariff prices; tariffs of 350 percent upheld to 2001 reach 1.0 Gt at 74 dollars per ton. Tariffs upheld to 2011 stay below 25 dollars per ton up to 4.0 Gt (tariffs of 175 percent). Unilateral long-run EU tariffs dominate coordinated short-run tariffs, and neither coordination nor commitment alone suffices.

  • Export taxes: taxes by Indonesia and Malaysia target the same traded goods as import tariffs, so they impose the same pressure to abate but keep the revenue at home, spare domestic consumers and require enforcement only at ports. They are welfare-enhancing for the exporters and more attractive than production taxes. The EU ranks production taxes above export taxes above EU-led import tariffs.

  • Carbon border adjustment: fixed import tariffs crowd out domestic regulation by shifting the burden of production taxes onto domestic consumers. With tariffs of 10 percent, modest production taxes reduce exporter welfare, and with tariffs of 50 percent all production taxes do. A carbon border adjustment mechanism that credits domestic regulation against the tariff restores the exporters' incentive to tax production.

The share equation is the Marshallian demand of the almost ideal demand system, obtained from a PIGLOG expenditure function by Shephard's lemma. Suppress the market index kkk where it is not needed and write γot=γok0+γok1t\gamma_{ot}=\gamma^0_{ok}+\gamma^1_{ok}tγot​=γok0​+γok1​t. The starting point is the log cost of reaching utility uuu at prices ptp_tpt​:

where ln⁡Pkt\ln P_{kt}lnPkt​ is the translog index of equation (2). Shephard's lemma says ∂ekt/∂pot=qokt\partial e_{kt}/\partial p_{ot}=q_{okt}∂ekt​/∂pot​=qokt​, so multiplying by pot/ektp_{ot}/e_{kt}pot​/ekt​ turns the log derivative of the cost function into the expenditure share:

ωokt=potqoktekt=∂ln⁡ekt∂ln⁡pot\omega_{okt}=\frac{p_{ot}q_{okt}}{e_{kt}}=\frac{\partial\ln e_{kt}}{\partial\ln p_{ot}}ωokt​=ekt​pot​qokt​​=∂lnpot​∂lnekt​​

Differentiate the two pieces separately. For the price index, the quadratic form contributes two symmetric terms, which collapse under the symmetry restriction αoo^k=αo^ok\alpha_{o\hat{o}k}=\alpha_{\hat{o}ok}αoo^k​=αo^ok​:

This is the translog price index that deflates expenditure in equation (1). These are the laws of motion of the two endogenous stocks of site iii. There is no depreciation term, so development is irreversible, and nit≥0n_{it}\geq0nit​≥0 means acreage never shrinks. The three-year lag is the source of time to build: revenue in equation (8) depends on NitN_{it}Nit​, so a hectare cleared today earns nothing until t+3t+3t+3, while its carbon is released immediately in equation (14). This timing drives the commitment problem. A tax in years ttt, t+1t+1t+1 or t+2t+2t+2 cannot affect the revenue of land cleared in ttt; only taxes expected from t+3t+3t+3 onward matter, as the term pt+3yit+3p_{t+3}y_{it+3}pt+3​yit+3​ in the Euler equation (17) makes explicit. Equation (7) is the Bellman equation of a site with a mill. Its useful implications are a first-order condition for nitn_{it}nit​ and the fact that this choice does not depend on existing acreage. Substituting back, the value function is additively separable: existing and pipeline acreage earn their revenues, and each future batch of development earns its surplus λn−c\lambda n-cλn−c, which at the optimum is (κ+ψn)n−(κ+12ψn)n=12ψn2(\kappa+\psi n)n-(\kappa+\tfrac{1}{2}\psi n)n=\tfrac{1}{2}\psi n^2(κ+ψn)n−(κ+21​ψn)n=21​ψn2. V(0,sit)=E[∑j≥0βj 12ψnit+j2∣sit]V(0,s_{it})=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j\geq0}\beta^j\,\tfrac{1}{2}\psi n_{it+j}^2\mid s_{it}\right]V(0,sit​)=E[j≥0∑​βj21​ψnit+j2​∣sit​]

Note that equation (7) writes the endogenous state as NitN_{it}Nit​ only, although acreage in the pipeline, Nit+1N_{it+1}Nit+1​ and Nit+2N_{it+2}Nit+2​, is also a state; by the linearity just shown this shorthand does not affect the optimal policy.

These are the flow payoffs of a site with a mill. Revenue rrr is the world price ptp_tpt​ (dollars per ton) times yield yity_{it}yit​ (tons per hectare) times mature acreage NitN_{it}Nit​ (hectares), scaled by α>0\alpha>0α>0. The coefficient α\alphaα converts dollars into the utility units in which the logit shock of equation (6) has unit scale, so dividing any cost parameter by α\alphaα expresses it in dollars. Revenue is linear in NitN_{it}Nit​: there are no diminishing returns within a site and no age effects.

The development cost is paid upfront in the year of clearing and is sunk. Its marginal cost is linear in nitn_{it}nit​:

∂c(nit,sit)∂nit=γg0+γg1t+xiδ+εit+ψnit\frac{\partial c(n_{it},s_{it})}{\partial n_{it}}=\gamma^0_g+\gamma^1_gt+x_i\delta+\varepsilon_{it}+\psi n_{it}∂nit​∂c(nit​,sit​)​=γg0​+γg1​t+xi​δ+εit​+ψnit​

The intercept collects a regional fixed effect γg0\gamma^0_gγg0​, a regional trend γg1\gamma^1_gγg1​ (negative if development becomes cheaper over time), observed cost shifters xiδx_i\deltaxi​δ and the unobserved cost εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​. The slope ψ>0\psi>0ψ>0 makes costs convex in the amount developed within a year, which captures credit constraints and congestion in local factor markets. Convexity is what makes the intensive margin well defined: with ψ=0\psi=0ψ=0 the problem is linear and a site would develop all its land at once or none. With ψ>0\psi>0ψ>0 development is smoothed over years, and the supply response to a price change builds up gradually, which is why long-run elasticities exceed short-run ones. Linear revenue with quadratic cost also yields the linear Euler equation (18), where α/ψ\alpha/\psiα/ψ is the response of development to future revenue, and the term 12ψnit2\tfrac{1}{2}\psi n_{it}^221​ψnit2​ in equation (19).

This is the one-time cost of building a mill, paid in the year of construction. It mirrors the intercept of the plantation cost in equation (8), with bars marking mill parameters: a regional fixed effect γˉg0\bar{\gamma}^0_gγˉ​g0​, a regional linear trend γˉg1\bar{\gamma}^1_gγˉ​g1​, observed cost factors xix_ixi​ with loadings δˉ\bar{\delta}δˉ, and an unobserved cost εˉit\bar{\varepsilon}_{it}εˉit​. There is no quadratic term because the choice is binary. Mills earn no direct revenue; a mill matters only because it unlocks plantation development, so the payoff from entry in equation (6) is −cˉ(sit)+V(0,sit)-\bar{c}(s_{it})+V(0,s_{it})−cˉ(sit​)+V(0,sit​). The cost is expressed in the same utility units as revenue, so cˉ/α\bar{c}/\alphacˉ/α is in dollars (the estimated median is about 91 million dollars).

Interpreting cˉ\bar{c}cˉ as an upfront sunk cost, rather than a flow cost or scrap value, is motivated by the near absence of exit in the data. The regional effects absorb unobserved heterogeneity, including weakly enforced existing regulation. In estimation, the cost enters equation (19) in quasi-differenced form, because a site compares building now with building next year:

−cˉ(sit)+βcˉ(sit+1)=βγˉg1−(1−β)(γˉg0+γˉg1t+xiδˉ)−εˉit+βεˉit+1-\bar{c}(s_{it})+\beta\bar{c}(s_{it+1})=\beta\bar{\gamma}^1_g-(1-\beta)\left(\bar{\gamma}^0_g+\bar{\gamma}^1_gt+x_i\bar{\delta}\right)-\bar{\varepsilon}_{it}+\beta\bar{\varepsilon}_{it+1}−cˉ(sit​)+βcˉ(sit+1​)=βγˉ​g1​−(1−β)(γˉ​g0​+γˉ​g1​t+xi​δˉ)−εˉit​+βεˉit+1​

The parameters γˉg0\bar{\gamma}^0_gγˉ​g0​ and δˉ\bar{\delta}δˉ are therefore identified only through the discount factor, from the level of entry rates across regions and across sites with different xix_ixi​, while γˉg1\bar{\gamma}^1_gγˉ​g1​ is identified from how entry rates drift over time.

Output of site iii in year ttt, in tons of palm oil, is yield yity_{it}yit​ times mature acreage NitN_{it}Nit​. There is no variable input choice and no capacity utilization margin: once land is planted and mature, it produces at the exogenous yield, so revenue in equation (8) is simply αptqitS\alpha p_tq^S_{it}αpt​qitS​. All supply responses therefore come from investment, through mill construction and plantation development.

Substituting the law of motion from equation (4) shows why supply is dynamic:

qitS=yit(Ni0+∑τ≤t−3niτ)q^S_{it}=y_{it}\left(N_{i0}+\sum_{\tau\leq t-3}n_{i\tau}\right)qitS​=yit​(Ni0​+τ≤t−3∑​niτ​)

Output today is predetermined by choices made at least three years ago, so the supply elasticity with respect to the current price alone is zero. Each past choice niτn_{i\tau}niτ​ was in turn forward-looking, responding to the expected discounted revenue from year τ+3\tau+3τ+3 onward. Hence qitSq^S_{it}qitS​ depends on prices before ttt only through the expectations they shaped, and on the whole expected price path, which is why world supply in equation (11) is written as a function of p1Tp_1^Tp1T​. This also explains the gap between short- and long-run elasticities (1.3 for a price change sustained to 2001 against 2.8 for one sustained to 2016): a temporary price change or tax moves few of the terms in the discounted sum that drives development.

These are the aggregation identities that turn market-level demand and site-level supply into world demand and supply. The first line sums the quantities demanded from equation (3) over the four consumer markets kkk for each oil ooo. Demand in market kkk depends on the two current world prices and on that market's expenditure XktX_{kt}Xkt​, which is treated as exogenous; all markets face the same world prices, since existing tariffs and trade costs are absorbed by the unobservables of equation (1).

The second line sums the output of equation (10) over the 2,050 sites. The argument is the entire path of palm prices p1Tp_1^Tp1T​, not p1tp_{1t}p1t​, because acreage is a stock of forward-looking choices, and it also depends on the path of yields yiTy_i^TyiT​. Only palm oil has a modeled supply side; the supply of other oils is an exogenous sequence S2tS_{2t}S2t​.

The asymmetry between the two lines carries the paper's two themes. World demand is a sum over markets, so a tariff that covers only some kkk leaves the other terms free to expand when the world price falls: this is demand-side leakage, the coordination problem. World supply is a function of the whole price path, so a tax that covers only some years moves supply little: this is the commitment problem. In the simulations, supply from Indonesia and Malaysia is scaled by a factor Ωt\Omega_tΩt​ to stand in for world supply, so the condition actually imposed is

D1t=ΩtS1tD_{1t}=\Omega_tS_{1t}D1t​=Ωt​S1t​

Market clearing defines the dynamic competitive equilibrium: a path of the two prices for t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,Tt=1,…,T such that, in every year, world palm oil demand equals world palm oil supply and world demand for other oils equals their exogenous supply. With TTT years there are 2T2T2T equations in 2T2T2T unknown prices.

The second condition is static: given p1tp_{1t}p1t​, it pins down p2tp_{2t}p2t​ year by year. The first is not, because S1tS_{1t}S1t​ depends on the whole path p1Tp_1^Tp1T​. Supply in year ttt depends on acreage chosen in earlier years on the basis of expected prices, including prices after ttt, so the equations cannot be solved one year at a time. The equilibrium is a fixed point in the price path: under rational expectations with no aggregate uncertainty in the solved model, the path sites expect must be the path that clears markets given the investment those expectations induce.

Each site is a price taker, but the two exporters together supply most of the world market and each importing bloc is large, so policies move p1tp_{1t}p1t​. This is the source of terms-of-trade effects in the counterfactuals: a production tax raises the world price to the benefit of the exporters, while an import tariff lowers it to the benefit of importers. Equation (13) is the same system with tax wedges inserted. In stylized form, with one period and one good, the condition reduces to the familiar

D(p∗)=S(p∗)D(p^*)=S(p^*)D(p∗)=S(p∗)

and the content of the model is that SSS responds to future as well as current prices.

The condition follows from equation (12) by replacing the single world price with the prices that consumers and producers actually face. An ad valorem consumption tax drives a wedge between the world price and the consumer price in market kkk, and an ad valorem production tax drives a wedge between the world price and the producer price in region ggg:

pktC=(1+τktD)p1t,pgtP=(1−τgtS)p1tp^C_{kt}=\left(1+\tau^D_{kt}\right)p_{1t},\qquad p^P_{gt}=\left(1-\tau^S_{gt}\right)p_{1t}pktC​=(1+τktD​)p1t​,pgtP​=(1−τgtS​)p1t​

Consumers choose shares and quantities from equations (1) to (3) at pktCp^C_{kt}pktC​, which gives the left-hand side. Producers earn revenue αpgtPyitNit\alpha p^P_{gt}y_{it}N_{it}αpgtP​yit​Nit​ in equation (8), so every price in the path that determines supply is replaced by its after-tax counterpart, which gives the right-hand side. In particular, the marginal value of development from the first-order condition of equation (7) becomes

λit=E[∑j≥3βjα(1−τg,t+jS)pt+jyit+j∣sit]\lambda_{it}=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j\geq3}\beta^j\alpha\left(1-\tau^S_{g,t+j}\right)p_{t+j}y_{it+j}\mid s_{it}\right]λit​=E[j≥3∑​βjα(1−τg,t+jS​)pt+j​yit+j​∣sit​]

Taxes in years ttt, t+1t+1t+1 and t+2t+2t+2 do not appear: development in ttt, and hence emissions in ttt, respond only to taxes expected from t+3t+3t+3 onward, and a tax that lapses after a short period removes only a few terms of the sum. This is the commitment problem in one line.

The equivalence between tariffs and production taxes follows from the ratio of consumer to producer prices, which is all that matters for quantities:

pktCpgtP=1+τktD1−τgtS\frac{p^C_{kt}}{p^P_{gt}}=\frac{1+\tau^D_{kt}}{1-\tau^S_{gt}}pgtP​pktC​​=1−τgtS​1+τktD​​

A consumption tax τD\tau^DτD in all markets and a production tax τS\tau^SτS in all regions give the same ratio when

1+τD=11−τS⟺τD=τS1−τS1+\tau^D=\frac{1}{1-\tau^S}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\tau^D=\frac{\tau^S}{1-\tau^S}1+τD=1−τS1​⟺τD=1−τSτS​

so τS=0.5\tau^S=0.5τS=0.5 corresponds to τD=1\tau^D=1τD=1. If p′p'p′ clears the market under the tariff, then p′′=(1+τD)p′p''=(1+\tau^D)p'p′′=(1+τD)p′ clears it under the equivalent production tax: consumers pay (1+τD)p′(1+\tau^D)p'(1+τD)p′ and producers receive p′p'p′ in both cases. The world price and the government that collects the revenue differ, which is why the two policies have opposite distributional effects. The equivalence fails for import tariffs proper, because they leave consumers in Indonesia and Malaysia untaxed.

Cumulative emissions are the carbon released by all plantation development over the study period. The term eie_iei​ is the carbon stock density of site iii in tons of CO2 per hectare, the sum of tree biomass and peat (1,626 tons on average, of which 1,240 in peat), and nitn_{it}nit​ is the number of hectares cleared in year ttt, so einite_in_{it}ei​nit​ is in tons and EEE sums over sites and years.

The formula embodies three assumptions. Carbon stocks are released fully and immediately when land is developed, so emissions are dated by nitn_{it}nit​ and not by mature acreage NitN_{it}Nit​ or output qitSq^S_{it}qitS​. Emissions are a one-time stock loss: producing palm oil on land already cleared emits nothing further. And development is irreversible, with no regrowth. Together these make emissions sunk, which is the root of the commitment problem: once nitn_{it}nit​ has occurred, no later policy can undo einite_in_{it}ei​nit​, so a regulator has no static reason to keep taxing.

A policy changes emissions only through development, weighted by carbon density:

ΔE=∑t∑iei Δnit\Delta E=\sum_t\sum_ie_i\,\Delta n_{it}ΔE=t∑​i∑​ei​Δnit​

A uniform tax on palm oil lowers nitn_{it}nit​ through the price terms in equation (18) regardless of eie_iei​, so it does not steer development away from carbon-rich peatland; the estimates also show that carbon stocks have negligible effects on private costs. ΔE\Delta EΔE is the denominator of the abatement cost in equation (15).

The first expression decomposes the welfare change of market kkk, relative to business as usual, into three parts measured in dollars. ΔCSk\Delta CS_kΔCSk​ is the change in consumer surplus, computed as a compensating variation from the expenditure function behind equations (1) and (2): the extra spending needed to reach baseline utility u0u^0u0 at the new consumer prices p1p^1p1,

ΔCSkt=−[ekt(u0,p1)−ekt(u0,p0)]\Delta CS_{kt}=-\left[e_{kt}\left(u^0,p^1\right)-e_{kt}\left(u^0,p^0\right)\right]ΔCSkt​=−[ekt​(u0,p1)−ekt​(u0,p0)]

ΔPSk\Delta PS_kΔPSk​ is the change in producer surplus, revenue net of mill and plantation costs, and is zero for markets that do not produce palm oil. ΔGRk\Delta GR_kΔGRk​ is tax revenue, the product of the tax rate, the world price and the taxed quantity (consumption for a tariff, production for a production tax). Tax payments are transfers: they lower consumer or producer surplus and raise government revenue, and which government collects them determines who gains.

The second expression divides the summed welfare change by the change in emissions from equation (14). Both are negative for a costly policy that abates, so the ratio is a positive number of dollars per ton of CO2. Climate benefits are deliberately left out of ΔWk\Delta W_kΔWk​, so that the cost can be compared with any social cost of carbon. A global planner favors the policy when the value of abatement exceeds the welfare loss, and for ΔE<0\Delta E<0ΔE<0 this is the same as the abatement cost lying below the social cost of carbon:

SCC⋅(−ΔE)+∑kΔWk>0⟺∑kΔWkΔE<SCCSCC\cdot(-\Delta E)+\sum_k\Delta W_k>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{\sum_k\Delta W_k}{\Delta E}<SCCSCC⋅(−ΔE)+k∑​ΔWk​>0⟺ΔE∑k​ΔWk​​<SCC

For example, the coordinated long-run production tax of 50 percent abates 7.4 Gt at 13 dollars per ton, a global loss of roughly 96 billion dollars.

This is the estimating equation for demand. It is equation (1) with the true price index PktP_{kt}Pkt​, which depends on the unknown parameters through equation (2), replaced by a fixed value Pkt0P^0_{kt}Pkt0​. Conditional on Pkt0P^0_{kt}Pkt0​ the equation is linear in αoo^k\alpha_{o\hat{o}k}αoo^k​, γok0\gamma^0_{ok}γok0​, γok1\gamma^1_{ok}γok1​ and δok\delta_{ok}δok​, so it can be estimated by linear instrumental variables. The iterated linear least squares procedure starts from a unit-value index,

ln⁡Pkt0=ln⁡Xkt−ln⁡Qkt,Qkt=∑oqokt\ln P^0_{kt}=\ln X_{kt}-\ln Q_{kt},\qquad Q_{kt}=\sum_oq_{okt}lnPkt0​=lnXkt​−lnQkt​,Qkt​=o∑​qokt​

estimates the linear equation, rebuilds the index from equation (2) with the new estimates, and repeats until the parameters stop changing; at the fixed point the estimates satisfy the nonlinear system of equations (1) and (2).

Only the palm oil share equation is estimated, separately for each market, because adding-up, homogeneity and symmetry tie down the other equation: the regressor is in effect the relative price ln⁡(p1t/p2t)\ln(p_{1t}/p_{2t})ln(p1t​/p2t​), with coefficient α11k\alpha_{11k}α11k​. Identification comes from annual time-series variation within a market. Prices are endogenous because a positive demand shock εokt\varepsilon_{okt}εokt​ raises prices, which biases the least squares estimate of the price response toward zero. The instruments are weather shocks to palm and to other-oil production, which shift supply; the exclusion restriction is that they affect expenditure shares only through prices. The estimated α11k\alpha_{11k}α11k​ and δ1k\delta_{1k}δ1k​ then determine the demand elasticities, as in the formula derived for equation (3), and hence the size of leakage.

The Euler equation compares developing a marginal hectare in year ttt with developing it in year t+1t+1t+1. Start from the first-order condition derived for equation (7), where κit=γg0+γg1t+xiδ+εit\kappa_{it}=\gamma^0_g+\gamma^1_gt+x_i\delta+\varepsilon_{it}κit​=γg0​+γg1​t+xi​δ+εit​ and λit\lambda_{it}λit​ is the expected discounted revenue of a hectare developed in ttt:

κit+ψnit=λit,λit=E[∑j≥3βjαpt+jyit+j∣sit]\kappa_{it}+\psi n_{it}=\lambda_{it},\qquad\lambda_{it}=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j\geq3}\beta^j\alpha p_{t+j}y_{it+j}\mid s_{it}\right]κit​+ψnit​=λit​,λit​=E[j≥3∑​βjαpt+j​yit+j​∣sit​]

The marginal value depends on the entire future, which is not observed. Split off the first term of the sum and recognize the remainder as the discounted value of a hectare developed one year later, using the law of iterated expectations:

λit=αβ3 E[pt+3yit+3∣sit]+β E[E[∑j≥3βjαpt+1+jyit+1+j∣sit+1]∣sit]=αβ3 E[pt+3yit+3∣sit]+β E[λit+1∣sit]\begin{aligned} \lambda_{it}&=\alpha\beta^3\,\mathbb{E}\left[p_{t+3}y_{it+3}\mid s_{it}\right]+\beta\,\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j\geq3}\beta^{j}\alpha p_{t+1+j}y_{it+1+j}\mid s_{it+1}\right]\mid s_{it}\right]\\ &=\alpha\beta^3\,\mathbb{E}\left[p_{t+3}y_{it+3}\mid s_{it}\right]+\beta\,\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda_{it+1}\mid s_{it}\right] \end{aligned}λit​​=αβ3E[pt+3​yit+3​∣sit​]+βE[E[j≥3∑​βjαpt+1+j​yit+1+j​∣sit+1​]∣sit​]=αβ3E[pt+3​yit+3​∣sit​]+βE[λit+1​∣sit​]​

A hectare developed in ttt rather than t+1t+1t+1 matures one year earlier, so it earns exactly one extra year of revenue, that of year t+3t+3t+3; from t+4t+4t+4 onward the two hectares are identical. Now use the first-order condition in t+1t+1t+1, λit+1=κit+1+ψnit+1\lambda_{it+1}=\kappa_{it+1}+\psi n_{it+1}λit+1​=κit+1​+ψnit+1​, to replace the unobserved continuation value with next year's marginal cost:

κit+ψnit=αβ3 E[pt+3yit+3∣sit]+β E[κit+1+ψnit+1∣sit]\kappa_{it}+\psi n_{it}=\alpha\beta^3\,\mathbb{E}\left[p_{t+3}y_{it+3}\mid s_{it}\right]+\beta\,\mathbb{E}\left[\kappa_{it+1}+\psi n_{it+1}\mid s_{it}\right]κit​+ψnit​=αβ3E[pt+3​yit+3​∣sit​]+βE[κit+1​+ψnit+1​∣sit​]

Writing out κit\kappa_{it}κit​ and κit+1\kappa_{it+1}κit+1​ gives equation (17), which the note states without the expectation operators and which holds in expectation conditional on sits_{it}sit​:

γg0+γg1t+xiδ+εit+ψnit=αβ3pt+3yit+3+β(γg0+γg1(t+1)+xiδ+εit+1+ψnit+1)\begin{aligned} &\gamma^0_g+\gamma^1_gt+x_i\delta+\varepsilon_{it}+\psi n_{it}\\ &\qquad=\alpha\beta^3p_{t+3}y_{it+3}+\beta\left(\gamma^0_g+\gamma^1_g(t+1)+x_i\delta+\varepsilon_{it+1}+\psi n_{it+1}\right) \end{aligned}​γg0​+γg1​t+xi​δ+εit​+ψnit​=αβ3pt+3​yit+3​+β(γg0​+γg1​(t+1)+xi​δ+εit+1​+ψnit+1​)​

The same condition follows from a perturbation argument: raise nitn_{it}nit​ by one hectare and lower nit+1n_{it+1}nit+1​ by one hectare, leaving acreage unchanged from t+4t+4t+4 on. The cost today is the left-hand side; the gain is one year of revenue plus the discounted saving of next year's marginal cost. At an interior optimum the perturbation has zero net value. The derivation needs interior solutions in both years and no age effects on revenue.

The regression equation rearranges the Euler equation (17) and replaces expectations with realizations. Start from the conditional-expectation form of equation (17), with κit=γg0+γg1t+xiδ+εit\kappa_{it}=\gamma^0_g+\gamma^1_gt+x_i\delta+\varepsilon_{it}κit​=γg0​+γg1​t+xi​δ+εit​:

κit+ψnit=αβ3 E[pt+3yit+3∣sit]+β E[κit+1+ψnit+1∣sit]\kappa_{it}+\psi n_{it}=\alpha\beta^3\,\mathbb{E}\left[p_{t+3}y_{it+3}\mid s_{it}\right]+\beta\,\mathbb{E}\left[\kappa_{it+1}+\psi n_{it+1}\mid s_{it}\right]κit​+ψnit​=αβ3E[pt+3​yit+3​∣sit​]+βE[κit+1​+ψnit+1​∣sit​]

ηit=αβ3ψ(E[pt+3yit+3∣sit]−pt+3yit+3)+βψ(E[εit+1+ψnit+1∣sit]−εit+1−ψnit+1)\eta_{it}=\frac{\alpha\beta^3}{\psi}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[p_{t+3}y_{it+3}\mid s_{it}\right]-p_{t+3}y_{it+3}\right)+\frac{\beta}{\psi}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\varepsilon_{it+1}+\psi n_{it+1}\mid s_{it}\right]-\varepsilon_{it+1}-\psi n_{it+1}\right)ηit​=ψαβ3​(E[pt+3​yit+3​∣sit​]−pt+3​yit+3​)+ψβ​(E[εit+1​+ψnit+1​∣sit​]−εit+1​−ψnit+1​)

so that

ψnit−βψnit+1=αβ3pt+3yit+3+βκit+1−κit+ψηit\psi n_{it}-\beta\psi n_{it+1}=\alpha\beta^3p_{t+3}y_{it+3}+\beta\kappa_{it+1}-\kappa_{it}+\psi\eta_{it}ψnit​−βψnit+1​=αβ3pt+3​yit+3​+βκit+1​−κit​+ψηit​

Next simplify the quasi-difference of the cost intercepts. The time-invariant parts are multiplied by β−1\beta-1β−1, and the trend contributes an extra βγg1\beta\gamma^1_gβγg1​ because next year's cost is one trend step further along:

βκit+1−κit=β(γg0+γg1(t+1)+xiδ)−(γg0+γg1t+xiδ)+βεit+1−εit=βγg1−(1−β)(γg0+γg1t+xiδ)−εit+βεit+1\begin{aligned} \beta\kappa_{it+1}-\kappa_{it}&=\beta\left(\gamma^0_g+\gamma^1_g(t+1)+x_i\delta\right)-\left(\gamma^0_g+\gamma^1_gt+x_i\delta\right)+\beta\varepsilon_{it+1}-\varepsilon_{it}\\ &=\beta\gamma^1_g-(1-\beta)\left(\gamma^0_g+\gamma^1_gt+x_i\delta\right)-\varepsilon_{it}+\beta\varepsilon_{it+1} \end{aligned}βκit+1​−κit​​=β(γg0​+γg1​(t+1)+xi​δ)−(γg0​+γg1​t+xi​δ)+βεit+1​−εit​=βγg1​−(1−β)(γg0​+γg1​t+xi​δ)−εit​+βεit+1​​

The structural errors are the parts of the regression residuals that come from unobserved costs, and they fall out of the quasi-differencing steps in equations (18) and (19).
